task.goal: Produce a single-frame numbered-grid body-signs SuperVisual where a hook headline and a labeled anatomical comparison grid carry the full activative payload without multi-slide sequencing, animation, or video motion.
task.success_condition: The hook headline reads as the scroll-stopping first beat at mobile scale, the six numbered tiles remain visually distinct with each caption legible against its photo, the viewer reads the grid as one bounded self-comparison chart rather than a sequence of separate posts, and the reassurance framing in the headline is not contradicted by the certainty of the tile captions.
task.atomic_boundary: One source claim set (a numbered visual-tile-to-label mapping) becomes one hook-plus-grid SuperVisual frame. No multi-slide carousel, no animation, no video, no chat interface.

source_claim_set.description: The ordered set of numbered visual-tile-to-label claims the SuperVisual grid must render.

label.description: The one-line caption paired with the tile.

visual_reference_context.description: Design, typography, and photographic reference context governing hook-headline and grid-tile composition.

supervisual_frame.description: A single production-ready image frame containing the hook headline and the numbered comparison grid.

activative_input.hidden_pressure: The viewer has scrolled past dozens of confident 'what your body says about you' graphics that turn ordinary anatomy into a checklist of things to worry about; this one must let curiosity resolve into reassurance, not new anxiety, without turning preachy or clinical.
activative_input.stance: Playful and observational, de-escalating rather than alarming.
stakes: an unverified visual comparison gets mistaken for a medical diagnosis
ordinary anatomical variation gets reframed as a personal health problem
identity_urges: understand my own body a little better
confirm I'm not the only one who looks like this
activative_input.participation_design: The viewer scans the six tiles, locates the one closest to their own belly button, reads its one-line label, and exhales — the grid format itself, not a call-to-action, delivers the payoff.
activative_input.intended_reaction: The viewer feels mildly informed and reassured, and either moves on or independently decides to ask a doctor if something genuinely concerns them — the graphic never tells them which.
activative_input.smallest_useful_commitment: Notice which numbered tile most resembles your own belly button.
wrong_reading_locks: Do not let the numbered, labeled grid format read as a validated medical diagnostic chart — it must stay legible as an illustrative comparison, not a clinical reference poster, even though the layout visually resembles one.

Do not let any single tile's caption stand alone outside the full six-tile set — cropping one tile out (e.g. for a standalone repost) turns a relative visual comparison into an isolated, unqualified diagnostic claim.

Do not raise the certainty of the tile captions above the headline's own hedge ('says less about your health than you might think') — captions must not read as more confident or alarming than the headline's reassurance framing promises.
Do not apply decorative filters, gradients, or stylized color grading to the anatomical photo tiles that would obscure the specific visual detail each caption is describing.

Do not omit or soften tile 1 and tile 6 (hernia / poor healing) into vague language that erases the one real case where a viewer should see a doctor — the format must stay honest about the one or two tiles that are not purely cosmetic.
